newsitem.title: USA: Alaska governor touts $2.4 billion budget.
newsitem.headline: Alaska governor touts $2.4 billion budget.

text.p: His $2.4 billion budget for fiscal year 1998 is lean enough to help prepare for impending oil revenue declines, Alaska Gov. Tony Knowles said in his annual state-of-the-budget address, delivered Thursday night.

Although it represents only a $2.5 million cut from the fiscal 1997 budget, the 1998 plan brings state spending within 90 percent of his goal of a $100 million cut over three years, Knowles said in his speech to the state legislature.
The three-year, $100 million cut had been recommended in late 1995 by a bipartisan fiscal panel as part of a strategy to cope with declining revenues from maturing North Slope oil fields.

"The budget I propose for the coming year continues efforts we began two years ago to cut state spending," Knowles, a Democrat, said in his speech, which was delivered in the capitol in Juneau and broadcast statewide.
He said significant budget-cutting progress has been made already.
"In fact, it may come as a surprise that we're spending a lot less per-person today than we were nearbly two decades ago," he said.
In current dollars, the state spends $340 less per-capita today than in 1979, he said.

To help replace declining oil revenues, Knowles has pushed for a $1-a-pack tobacco tax increase, which would add to the state's current 29-cent-a-pack rate and give Alaska the nation's highest tobacco tax.
In his speech Thursday, the governor reiterated his call for the tax hike, which he said would discourage minors from smoking or chewing tobacco.
"This year, for our children, let's make Alaska's tobacco tax the straw that breaks Joe Camel's back," he said, crushing a pack of cigarettes in his hand.

He said it will be the only tax increase that he will introduce in this year's legislative session, a departure from last year's strategy, when he championed unsuccessful measures to raise taxes on alcohol and fuel.
Oil revenue accounts for over 80 percent of Alaska's general operating budget. Alaska has no state personal income tax, no state sales tax and the nation's lowest fuel tax.
It also has a unique program that pays an annual dividend check from an oil-trust account to all residents; the 1996 check was $1,130.

Earlier in the day, Alaska Revenue Commissioner Wilson Condon told a legislative committee that new production planned by British Petroleum unit BP Exploration (Alaska) Inc. and Atlantic Richfield unit Arco Alaska Inc. will cause oil revenues to stablize in the future instead of continuing to fall.
If the companies and their partners achieve their production goals, annual state oil revenues will stablize at about $1.9 billion in 2005, Condon told the state Senate finance committee.
For this year, the state is likely to reap benefits from unusually high prices for North Slope crude, he said.
"In the short term, the state is showing a budget surplus," he said.
The Department of Revenue's estimates of oil receipts have been boosted by $111 million for the 1997 fiscal year, which ends June 30, and $113 million for the 1998 fiscal year, Condon said.
